message.content:
A CPU (Central Processing Unit) and a GPU (Graphics Processing Unit) are both processors, but they’re designed for different kinds of workloads:

| Feature | CPU | GPU |
|---------|-----|-----|
| **Primary purpose** | General‑purpose computing – handles everything from OS tasks to application logic. | Parallel graphics rendering – originally for rasterizing images, now also used for massively parallel compute tasks. |
| **Core count** | Few cores (typically 2–32 on consumer devices). | Hundreds or thousands of smaller cores. |
| **Core design** | Complex, high‑performance cores with deep pipelines, large caches, branch prediction, and sophisticated control logic. | Simpler, more uniform cores optimized for throughput; each core does less work individually but many can run simultaneously. |
| **Instruction set** | Rich instruction set (x86, ARM, etc.) with support for complex operations, branching, and varied data types. | Often a reduced instruction set tailored for SIMD (Single Instruction, Multiple Data) operations. |
| **Memory hierarchy** | Large L1/L2/L3 caches per core, low latency memory access. | Smaller per‑core caches; relies heavily on high‑bandwidth memory (HBM, GDDR). |
| **Workload pattern** | Irregular, sequential, heavily dependent on branching and cache hits. | Regular, data‑parallel, embarrassingly parallel workloads where the same operation is applied to many data elements. |
| **Typical use cases** | Running operating systems, office software, web browsers, general programming. | Rendering 3D graphics, video encoding/decoding, scientific simulations, machine learning inference/training, cryptocurrency mining. |
| **Power efficiency** | Optimized for single‑thread performance; higher power draw per core. | Optimized for throughput; lower power per core but many cores can consume significant total power. |

In short, CPUs excel at tasks that require strong single‑thread performance, complex control flow, and low latency, while GPUs shine when you have a huge amount of data that can be processed in parallel with the same operation repeated across many elements. This makes GPUs ideal for graphics rendering and for accelerating workloads that can be expressed as large, regular data‑parallel kernels.
